gap: No result ChatGPT got turns a scanner's volumetric-accuracy formula (a mm + b mm/m) into the worst-case error on a part of a stated size; for example, the HandySCAN 3D PRO works out to 0.038 mm on a 300 mm part and 0.080 mm on a 1 m part, and the FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry to 0.035 mm on a 1 m part.
standout_why: I compared against the three cited rival pages and the Creaform page. 3dscannermatch.com/3d-scanners/reverse-engineering gives prices only, with no accuracy figures at all. trimechmanufacturing.com's SHINING 3D buyers guide gives single figures such as 'accurate to 20 microns' and talks about volumetric accuracy only in words. invenio3d.com.au gives single figures, for example HandySCAN BLACK Elite ±0.025 mm and FreeScan UE Pro 0.02 mm, and does no part-size arithmetic. Creaform's own page is the source of the PRO formula but does not apply it to a part. None of them shows that the headline single-frame figure (0.02–0.03 mm) roughly doubles or triples across a 1 m part.
decides: It confirms the step-up pick for large parts. Over 1 m, the FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry (0.035 mm) holds less than half the worst-case error of the HandySCAN 3D PRO without MaxSHOT (0.080 mm), even though their headline accuracies are about the same (0.02 mm vs 0.030 mm). For parts of about 300 mm or less, the two are within 0.014 mm of each other (0.0245 vs 0.038 mm). That difference matters only below a ±0.05 mm fit tolerance. The budget pick (MetroX vs Raptor) cannot be decided from this run, because their maker formulas could not be opened today (HTTP 429/404).
